title: Signs of life: why still plants and seeds are alive

summary.text: A bowl of moong sprouts lies still on the kitchen shelf. Shut them in a steel dabba for three hours, and they breathe out enough carbon dioxide to turn clear chuna water milky. Every kind of living being does seven things: eat, breathe, grow, move, sense, get rid of waste and have young. Plants do all seven, only slowly or out of sight. In this unit you catch sprouts breathing and sort tricky cases like a phone, a cloud, curd and a potato.
summary.art: A steel dabba with the lid lifted, a small glass of milky white water standing on a bed of moong sprouts inside, and a child peering in with wide eyes.

intro.hook: Put a bowl of moong sprouts next to a toy car. Push the car, and the car zooms across the floor. The sprouts just lie there. Which one is breathing?
intro.text: The car moves, but a car never breathes. The sprouts do not seem to do anything at all. Yet sprouts are alive, and every living being breathes. You cannot see breath, so we need a way to catch it. Chuna water is clear water that turns milky when breathed-out air reaches it. In this unit we use it to find out if still sprouts really breathe.
intro.art: A toy car on a kitchen floor next to a steel bowl of moong sprouts with tiny white tails, and a question mark above them.

outcomes: By the end I can name the seven signs of life in simple words: eat, breathe, grow, move, sense, get rid of waste and have young.
By the end I can show that plants are alive, even though they seem still, and give two signs of life in a plant.
By the end I can sort tricky cases, like a dry seed, curd, a phone or a cloud, and give a reason for each.
By the end I can say why one sign of life alone does not show that something is alive.
By the end I can do a fair test with two dabbas, and say what I think, what I saw and why.
By the end I can explain that living beings breathe out carbon dioxide, even when they are still.

terms.meaning: The signs of life are seven things that every kind of living being does: eat, breathe, grow, move, sense, get rid of waste and have young. Scientists call them the life processes.
terms.example: A crow does all seven. A moong plant does all seven too, more slowly.
terms.art: Seven small pictures in a ring: a goat eating grass, a child breathing out, a sprout growing, a crow flying, an ear, a drop of sweat, a hen with chicks.

terms.meaning: Breathing is how a living being uses air to get energy from food. Every living being breathes, even plants and many tiny beings too small to see.
terms.example: You breathe through your nose. A plant breathes through tiny holes in their leaves, stem and roots.
terms.art: A child breathing out on one side, and a leaf with tiny holes drawn large on the other.

terms.meaning: Carbon dioxide is a gas that living beings breathe out. You cannot see it or smell it.
terms.example: When you blow into chuna water, the carbon dioxide in your breath turns the water milky.
terms.art: A child blowing through a straw into a small glass of water that is turning milky white.

terms.meaning: To sense is to notice what is around you, such as light, touch, sound, smell, heat or water.
terms.example: A cat senses a sound and turns her ears. A potato shoot senses where the light is and grows that way.
terms.art: A cat with ears turned towards a bell, and a potato with a pale shoot reaching towards a crack of light.

terms.meaning: Waste is what a body makes but does not need, so the body gets rid of it.
terms.example: You get rid of waste when you breathe out, sweat and go to the toilet. A plant lets out extra water and oxygen through their leaves.
terms.art: A child breathing out and a tulsi plant with tiny drops and small bubbles drawn rising from a leaf.

terms.meaning: To have young is to make new living beings of your own kind. Scientists call this reproduction.
terms.example: A hen lays eggs that hatch into chicks. A mango tree makes mangoes with a seed inside each one.
terms.art: A hen with chicks, and a mango cut open to show the big seed inside.

terms.meaning: Chuna water is clear water with a little chuna, the white lime paste used with paan, mixed in. Scientists call it limewater. It turns milky white when carbon dioxide reaches it.
terms.example: Blow your breath into chuna water through a straw, and in about one minute the water goes milky.
terms.art: Two small glasses side by side: one with clear water, one with milky white water, and a straw in the milky one.

terms.meaning: A fair test changes only one thing and keeps everything else the same. Then we know what made the difference.
terms.example: Two dabbas got the same chuna water, the same wet cloth and the same place. Only one had sprouts.
terms.art: Two identical steel dabbas side by side, one with sprouts inside and one with only a wet cloth.

explanations.context: This card lists the seven things that every kind of living being does.
explanations.definition: A living being eats, breathes, grows, moves, senses, gets rid of waste and has young. Scientists call these the seven life processes.
explanations.description: Every kind of living being does all seven, in their own way. A sparrow does them quickly, so we notice them. A neem tree does them slowly, so we miss most of them. A baby cannot have young yet, but will be able to as a grown-up.
examples: A goat eats grass, breathes, grows, walks, hears her kid call, makes dung and has kids.
A neem tree makes food in their leaves, breathes, grows taller, turns their leaves to the light, senses water with their roots, drops old leaves and makes seeds.
You do all seven every day, except having young, which comes later.
explanations.art: A goat and a neem tree side by side, with seven small icons beside each one.

explanations.concept: Plants are alive, even though they seem still
explanations.context: This card is about why plants are alive, though they never seem to do anything.
explanations.definition: Plants do all seven signs of life. They do them slowly, or in places we cannot see.
explanations.description: Plants make their own food in their green leaves, using sunlight, air and water. They breathe all day and all night. They move by growing: shoots bend towards light, and roots grow down towards water. In our dabba test, still sprouts breathed out carbon dioxide and turned chuna water milky.
examples: Moong sprouts in a shut dabba turn chuna water milky in a few hours.
A potato left in a dark cupboard grows pale shoots towards the crack of light at the door.
A karela vine curls a thin tendril tightly round a string they touch.
explanations.art: A karela vine on a balcony grill, with a thin green tendril coiled round a string.

explanations.concept: Tricky cases: one sign is not enough
explanations.context: This card is about things that seem alive but are not, and things that seem not alive but are.
explanations.definition: A living being does all seven signs of life, in their own way. Something that cannot do them, like a car or a cloud, is not alive.
explanations.description: A toy car moves, but a car never eats, grows or has young. A cloud grows and moves, but a cloud never eats or breathes. A phone senses your touch, but a phone never grows. A dry moong seed seems to do nothing, but the seed is alive and resting. Give the seed water, and they wake up and grow.
examples: A ceiling fan moves, but was never alive.
A potato in the cupboard looks like food, but is alive and can grow a whole new plant.
A spoon of curd looks like food, but is full of tiny living beings.
explanations.art: A table with tricky things in a row: a toy car, a cloud drawn on card, a phone, a dry moong seed, a potato with shoots and a bowl of curd.

explanations.context: This card is about a tricky case from the kitchen: curd.
explanations.definition: Curd is full of tiny living beings called bacteria. Bacteria are living beings far too small to see without a microscope.
explanations.description: When you add a spoon of curd to warm milk, the bacteria in the curd eat the sugar in the milk. They grow and split into more bacteria. As they eat, they turn the milk thick and sour. That is how milk becomes curd overnight.
examples: A spoon of curd in warm milk sets a whole bowl of curd by the next morning.
Milk that is too hot kills the bacteria, and then the milk does not set.
Idli batter rises overnight because of tiny living beings too.
explanations.art: A katori of curd with a small circle zooming in to show tiny bacteria.

explanations.context: This card is about whether plants feel and decide, or only react.
explanations.description: Plants sense light, touch, water and warmth, and they act on what they sense. A potato shoot chooses the way to the light. A karela tendril chooses a string to hold. Plants feel, remember and decide, in their own way. Other scientists call these actions automatic.
examples: A potato shoot in a box grows round corners to reach a hole of light.
A karela tendril that touches nothing stays straight. A tendril that touches a string coils round it.
Roots grow towards wet soil and away from dry soil.

perspectives.who: Many scientists who study plant behaviour
perspectives.explanation: Plants sense, remember and decide. They pick where to grow, using what they sense, much as animals pick where to go.
Plants have no brain, so their actions are automatic, like a door that opens when you step near it.

explanations.art: A shoebox cut open to show a pale potato shoot winding round two card walls towards a hole of light.

agreed.text: Plants breathe all the time, day and night.
agreed.evidence: Scientists measure the gases around plants in light and in the dark. Plants always give out carbon dioxide from breathing. In sunlight, their leaves also take in carbon dioxide to make food, so we do not notice the breathing then.

agreed.text: Every kind of living being does all seven signs of life.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have studied many kinds of living beings, from bacteria to whales and banyan trees. Every kind eats, breathes, grows, moves, senses, gets rid of waste and has young.

agreed.text: Curd is set by living bacteria.
agreed.evidence: Boiled milk with no curd added stays milk. Boiled milk with a spoon of curd sets. Under a microscope, curd is full of tiny bacteria.

challenging.claim: A seed or a potato that does nothing is not alive.
challenging.who: A common idea among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: A dry seed or a potato in a basket does not move, eat or grow for weeks.
challenging.against: Give a seed water, or leave a potato in a cupboard, and they grow. They were alive and resting all along. Soaked moong in a shut dabba turn chuna water milky, so they are breathing.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that still things are not alive.

challenging.who: A common mistake, found even in some books
challenging.for: At night, plants give out carbon dioxide and take in none. So the breathing is easy to measure then.
challenging.against: Plants breathe day and night. In sunlight they also make food, and that takes in more carbon dioxide than breathing gives out. So by day the breathing is hidden, not stopped.
challenging.context: This card is about when plants breathe.

challenging.claim: A phone that hears you and answers back is alive.
challenging.for: A phone senses touch and sound, and answers questions. Some phones learn your voice.
challenging.against: A phone never eats, grows or makes baby phones. A phone runs on electricity from a charger, and stops when the battery is empty.
challenging.context: This card is about a tricky case: a talking phone.

challenging.claim: Plants feel and choose, just as animals do.
challenging.who: Some plant scientists, and many traditions in India
challenging.for: Plants sense light, touch, water and sound, remember what happened before, and change what they do.
challenging.against: Other scientists call these actions automatic. They point out that plants have no brain or nerves, so they do not count this as feeling.
challenging.context: This card is about whether plants feel and choose.

big_questions.q: The sprouts breathed in a shut dabba. What do you think they were breathing in?
big_questions.hint: Think about the air inside the dabba. You breathe in the same air.

big_questions.q: If you never saw a potato grow, how could you find out the potato is alive?
big_questions.hint: Think of the signs of life you could test without waiting for shoots.

big_questions.q: Is a phone that learns your voice a little bit alive?
big_questions.hint: Go through the seven signs one by one. Which ones does the phone have?

big_questions.q: You breathe out carbon dioxide, and a plant takes carbon dioxide in. Where does your breath go after it leaves you?
big_questions.hint: Think of the plants near you, and the trees on the road.

big_questions.q: Could there be living beings so slow that we never notice they are alive?
big_questions.hint: Think of a tree that lives for 500 years. What would a whole day look like to them?

story.title: The Potato in the Dark Cupboard
story.note: Shalini, Nikhil and Ajji are made up. Kamala Sohonie was real. Potato shoots do grow towards light, and a sprouted potato planted in soil usually makes several new potatoes in about three months. Never eat potato shoots or green potato skin, because they contain a substance that can make people sick.
text: It was a Sunday morning in a flat in Bengaluru. Shalini's grandmother, Ajji, was making uppittu for breakfast. 'Shalini, please bring me one onion from the bottom cupboard,' she called.
Shalini was eight. She opened the low cupboard next to the stove. It was dark inside, and it smelled of onions and dust. She pushed the onion basket aside, and then she stopped.

Behind the basket, in the corner, sat an old potato. Long, thin shoots grew out of the potato's skin. They were pale white, with a little purple at the tips. Every single shoot was bent the same way, towards the crack of the cupboard door.
'Ajji! Nikhil! Come and look!' Shalini shouted.
Her little brother Nikhil came running. He was five. He peeped in and jumped back. 'Worms!' he cried. 'The potato has worms!'
Ajji came with the spoon still in her hand. She bent down and smiled. 'Those are not worms,' she said. 'Those are shoots. This potato has been growing, all by themselves, in the dark.'
Shalini frowned. 'But potatoes are food,' she said. 'Food is not alive.'
'Are you sure?' asked Ajji. 'What do living beings do?'
Shalini counted on her fingers. 'They eat. They breathe. They grow. They move. They sense things. They get rid of waste. They have young.'
'Good. Then let us check the potato,' said Ajji. 'Did the potato grow?'
'Yes,' said Shalini. 'Last month there were no shoots at all.'
'And where did the potato get food to grow them?' asked Ajji. 'There is no soil in the cupboard, and no water, and no sunlight.'

Shalini picked up the potato gently. The potato felt soft and wrinkly, not hard and smooth like a new one. 'From inside!' she said. 'The potato used the food stored inside, to make the shoots. That is why the potato is so soft now.'
Nikhil was still looking at the shoots. 'Why are they all pointing at the door?' he asked.
Shalini put the potato back in the corner. She closed the cupboard door, but not all the way. A thin line of light fell across the shoots, from the kitchen window.
'The light comes in through the crack,' she said slowly. 'The potato sensed the light. The shoots grew towards the light, so they moved, but very slowly.'
'That is right,' said Ajji. 'And here is a funny thing. The little dents that the shoots grow from are called the potato's eyes.'
Nikhil laughed. Then he folded his arms. 'But the potato cannot breathe,' he said. 'A potato has no nose.'
'You do not need a nose to breathe,' said Ajji. 'Every living being breathes, deep inside, in the tiny living parts their body is made of. Those tiny parts are called cells.'

She sat down on the kitchen stool. 'About ninety years ago, a young Indian scientist called Kamala Sohonie studied potatoes in a laboratory in England. She found that potato cells have a special substance that helps them breathe. Our own cells use the same kind of substance.'
'Was she from Bengaluru?' asked Shalini.

'She was born in Indore,' said Ajji. 'But she came to study at the big science institute here in Bengaluru. At first, the head of the institute tried to turn her away, because she was a woman. She would not go away. She worked so well that they had to let her stay. Later she became the first Indian woman to earn a PhD in science, the highest university degree.'
Shalini looked at the wrinkly potato in her hand. 'So the potato eats, breathes, grows, moves and senses,' she said. 'But can a potato have young?'
'Let us find out,' said Ajji.

After breakfast, they filled an old paint bucket with soil from the building's garden. Nikhil dug a hole. Shalini put the potato in, with the shoots pointing up, and covered the potato with soil. They put the bucket in the sunniest corner of the balcony.
Within a week, green stems pushed up out of the soil. In the sunlight, the pale shoots had turned green, and they opened small, crinkly leaves. Nikhil watered them every morning before school.
The plant grew tall and bushy. Then, after about three months, the leaves turned yellow and began to dry.
'Now,' said Ajji. She spread an old newspaper on the balcony floor and tipped the bucket over. Out came the soil, and in the soil were seven small new potatoes, round and smooth.
The old potato was there too. The old potato was shrivelled and empty, like a little brown bag.
Nikhil picked up a new potato in each hand. 'The old potato had babies!' he shouted.
'Seven of them,' said Shalini. Then she frowned again. 'What about waste? That is the last sign.'
'Every day, the leaves let out water and gases into the air,' said Ajji. 'The plant got rid of what they did not need. You just could not see it.'

Shalini sat back on her heels. All those weeks in the dark cupboard, the potato had looked like food, sitting still. But the potato had been alive the whole time, breathing, sensing the light and slowly reaching for it.
She looked through the kitchen door at the onion basket. 'Ajji,' she said, 'is the onion alive too?'
Ajji laughed. 'Put one on a glass of water and see,' she said.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Shalini checks the old potato against the signs of life one by one. The potato used stored food, grew, sensed the light and grew towards it, breathed, let out waste, and, planted in soil, made new potatoes. Something that looked like still food was alive all along.
ask: Why were all the potato shoots bent towards the cupboard door?
Why was the old potato soft and wrinkly?
Nikhil said a potato cannot breathe without a nose. What would you tell him?
Kamala Sohonie was almost turned away because she was a woman. Why do you think she would not go away?

games.title: Missing Signs: the tricky case card game
games.context: This is a card game about tricky cases. Each card names a thing. You say one sign of life the thing seems to show, and one sign that is missing. Then you decide: alive or not?

items.b: Seems to: move. Missing: eat, breathe, grow, sense, waste, young. Never alive.
Seems to: grow and move. Missing: eat, breathe, sense, young. Never alive.

items.f: A phone that answers when you talk
items.b: Seems to: sense sound and touch. Missing: eat, breathe, grow, young. Never alive.

items.f: A robot that cleans the floor
items.b: Seems to: move and sense walls. Missing: eat food, breathe, grow, young. Never alive.
Seems to: move. Missing: the other six signs. Never alive.
Seems to do nothing. But with water, the seed sprouts and grows. Alive, resting.

items.f: An old potato in the cupboard
items.b: Grows shoots towards light, breathes, can have young. Alive.
Full of tiny living bacteria that eat, grow and make more of themselves in milk. Alive inside.
Seems still. Breathing, heart beating, growing. Alive.

rules: Mix the 12 cards and put them in a pile in the middle, front side up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. A parent can read it for a child who cannot read it yet.
Say one sign of life the thing seems to show, and one sign that is missing.
Then say: alive, once alive or never alive.

Another player turns the card over and reads the back aloud. You score one point if the sign you said is missing is one of the missing signs on the back, and one point if your answer matches the back. Keep score with tally marks on a sheet of paper.
If the thing is alive, no sign is really missing, even if you cannot see it. Say "nothing missing" to win that point.
Play until all 12 cards are done. The player with the most points wins. If two players tie, they both win.

flow.do: 1. Print and cut out the 12 cards, or write the front and back of each on paper or old card. 2. Put out a sheet of paper and a pencil for scoring. 3. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: Each card is a tricky thing. You find one sign it seems to have, and one sign it is missing.
flow.kid: Read the card. Find one sign it has. Find one sign it is missing.

flow.do: Take turns. Read each back aloud and talk about any surprises.
flow.say: A cloud grows and moves. Which sign is missing? Is a cloud alive?
flow.kid: Read your card. Say a sign it has. Say a sign it is missing.

ask.q: Why is a dry moong seed alive, though the seed does nothing?
good: Because seeds sprout when you give them water.
Because seeds are resting, not dead.

flow.parent: The surprises are the point: a robot and a phone seem alive but are not, and a seed and a coconut seem not alive but are.

flow.do: Count the points. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Which card surprised you most? Why?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which card surprised you?

check.q: A robot moves and senses walls. Why is the robot not alive?
options: The robot does not eat, grow or have young
The robot is made of plastic
check.why: Moving and sensing are only two of the seven signs. A robot never eats food, grows or makes baby robots. One or two signs alone do not make something alive.

experiments.title: Do Still Sprouts Breathe? The chuna water test
experiments.context: In this experiment you shut moong sprouts in one steel dabba and only a wet cloth in another. Each dabba holds a small glass of chuna water. After three hours you look to see which chuna water has gone milky. This tells us if sprouts that lie still are breathing.
experiments.question: Moong sprouts lie still and do not seem to do anything. Do they breathe out carbon dioxide, like you do?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which chuna water will go milky: the one shut in with the sprouts, the one shut in with only a wet cloth, both, or neither? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both dabbas are the same size, with the same wet cloth, the same amount of chuna water, the same place and the same time. Only one has sprouts. So if one chuna water goes milky and the other does not, the sprouts made the difference.

materials.item: whole green moong, about half a cup (or about 1 cup of ready sprouted moong from the shop)
chuna, the plain white lime paste sold at paan shops and grocery shops, about half a teaspoon
a jug or bottle of about half a litre of water, and a plate to cover the jug
two steel dabbas of the same size with tight lids, big enough for a small glass to stand inside
three small clear glasses or cups, such as small chai glasses or medicine cups
two thin cotton cloths or handkerchiefs, made wet and squeezed out
a drinking straw
a dark cloth or a sheet of dark paper, to look at the glasses against

experiments.safety: Only a grown-up handles the chuna. Chuna can sting eyes and skin, so never taste it and wash hands after touching it. Never drink chuna water. When blowing through the straw, only blow out, never suck in. Do not eat the moong from the test afterwards.

schedule.what: In the evening, soak the moong in water. Stir the chuna into the jug of water and cover it with a plate. Leave both overnight.
Drain the moong. Blow into chuna water to see what milky looks like. Guess. Set up the two dabbas and close them.
Three hours later, open both dabbas. Compare the chuna water against a dark cloth. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Draw the two dabbas with their glasses, before and after. Colour the water that went milky white.

flow.do: 1. In the evening, put half a cup of moong in a bowl and cover with water. 2. Stir half a teaspoon of chuna into the jug of water. 3. Cover the jug with a plate. 4. Leave both overnight without stirring.
flow.say: Tonight we soak some moong. We also make chuna water. It must sit still all night, so the chalky part sinks.
flow.kid: Help soak the moong in water. A grown-up makes the chuna water.
flow.parent: By morning, the chalky part of the chuna sinks and the water on top looks clear. Only the clear top is used. If the water is still cloudy, pour the top through a clean cotton cloth. If you buy ready sprouted moong, you only need to make the chuna water.
flow.wait: Leave the moong and the chuna water overnight.

flow.do: 1. Drain the moong into a plate. 2. Let your child look closely and touch them. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Look at the moong now. They are fat from the water, and a few may have a tiny white tip. Are they doing anything? Do you think they are alive?
flow.kid: Look at the moong. Touch them. Are they doing anything? Are they alive?

ask.q: Are the moong doing anything?
good: They are just lying there.
They got fat from the water, and some may have a tiny tail.

flow.parent: Soaked moong swell overnight, and some push out a tiny white root tip. If yours have none, that is fine. Soaked moong are awake and breathing. Don't tell your child that yet.

flow.do: 1. Pour clear chuna water off the top of the jug into one small glass, about a quarter full. 2. Let your child blow gently through the straw into it for about one minute. 3. Look at the water.
flow.say: This clear water has chuna in it. Blow gently into it through the straw. Only blow out, never suck. Watch the water.
flow.kid: Blow gently through the straw. Only blow out. Watch the water.

ask.q: What happened to the water?
good: It went milky white.
It turned cloudy, like watery milk.

flow.parent: Practise blowing bubbles in plain water first, so your child only blows out. The water usually turns milky in under a minute. This is because your breath has carbon dioxide in it. If your child keeps blowing for many minutes, the water can go clear again, so stop once it is milky.

flow.do: Tell your child what you will do with the two dabbas. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write down the guess.
flow.say: Your breath turned chuna water milky. Now we shut sprouts in one dabba, and only a wet cloth in the other. Each gets a glass of chuna water. Which water will go milky? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Sprouts go in one dabba. Only a wet cloth goes in the other. Which water will go milky? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: The sprouts one, because the sprouts are alive and breathe.
Neither, because sprouts have no nose.
Both, because the wet cloth makes it milky.

flow.parent: Every guess is fine, as long as your child gives a reason. Don't hint at the answer.

flow.do: 1. Lay a wet cloth flat in each dabba. 2. Spread the moong on the cloth in the first dabba only. 3. Pour clear chuna water into two small glasses, the same amount in each. 4. Stand one glass in the middle of each dabba. 5. Close both lids tightly. 6. Put both dabbas side by side on a shelf, out of the sun.
flow.say: Both dabbas are the same, except one has sprouts. This makes it a fair test. Now we close the lids tight, so no room air gets in.
flow.kid: Put sprouts in one dabba only. Stand a glass in each. Close the lids tight.
flow.parent: Pour gently and don't splash chuna water onto the moong. Keep the glasses upright. The empty dabba shows what happens with no sprouts.

flow.do: Leave both dabbas shut for three hours. Read the story or play a game while you wait.
flow.say: Now we wait three hours without opening the lids.
flow.kid: Now we wait three hours. Don't open the lids.
flow.wait: Leave both dabbas shut for three hours.

flow.do: 1. Open both dabbas. 2. Lift out the glasses carefully. 3. Hold them side by side in front of the dark cloth. 4. Let your child smell inside each dabba too.
flow.say: Look at the two glasses against the dark cloth. What do you see? Is there any difference?
flow.kid: Hold the glasses in front of the dark cloth. What is different?

ask.q: Which chuna water changed?
good: The one with the sprouts went milky.
The sprout one has a white skin on top.

ask.q: What do you notice inside the sprout dabba?
good: It is damp.
It smells of sprouts.

flow.parent: The chuna water in the sprout dabba usually has a white skin on top and looks cloudy. The other one stays clear, or gets only a very thin skin from the air in the dabba. If you cannot see a difference after three hours, close the lids and look again after three more hours.

flow.do: Ask your child to say three things: what I think, what I saw, and why. Then draw the two dabbas together.
flow.say: So do still sprouts breathe? Tell me what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Do sprouts breathe? Say what you think. Say what you saw. Say why.

ask.q: Why did only one chuna water go milky?
good: Because the sprouts breathed out carbon dioxide, like I did with the straw.
Because the other dabba had nothing alive to breathe.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses the evidence: the sprout water went milky like the breath water, and the empty dabba stayed clear. Sprouts breathe out carbon dioxide all the time, as you do, even though they lie still.

check.q: The chuna water went milky in the sprout dabba, but not in the empty dabba. What does this show?
options: Wet cloth makes chuna water milky
The sprouts breathed out carbon dioxide
check.why: Both dabbas had a wet cloth and were steel, so those cannot be the reason. Only the sprout dabba changed. Your breath made chuna water milky too, because breath has carbon dioxide. So the sprouts were breathing out carbon dioxide.

rows: milky, with a white skin on top
clear, with a very thin skin
milky after one minute of blowing

experiments.title: Cold Sprouts: do sprouts breathe more slowly in the fridge?
experiments.context: In this experiment you do the chuna water test again, with two dabbas of sprouts. One dabba goes in the fridge and one stays on the shelf. Then you compare how milky the two chuna waters get.
experiments.question: Do sprouts breathe as much in the cold fridge as on a warm shelf?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which chuna water will go more milky: the one in the fridge or the one on the shelf? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both dabbas get the same amount of sprouts, the same wet cloth and the same amount of chuna water, for the same time. Only the place is different: one is cold and one is warm.

materials.item: whole green moong, about 1 cup, soaked overnight
clear chuna water, made the night before (half a teaspoon of chuna stirred into half a litre of water, in a jug with a plate over it, left to settle overnight)
two steel dabbas of the same size with tight lids
two small clear glasses
two wet cotton cloths
a dark cloth, to look at the glasses against

experiments.safety: Only a grown-up handles the chuna and the chuna water. Never taste or drink it, and wash hands after.

schedule.what: In the evening, soak 1 cup of moong. Make chuna water and cover it.
Set up two sprout dabbas. Put one in the fridge and one on a shelf. After three hours, compare the two chuna waters.

experiments.record: Draw the fridge dabba and the shelf dabba with their glasses. Colour how milky each one went.

flow.do: 1. In the evening, soak 1 cup of moong in water. 2. Stir half a teaspoon of chuna into half a litre of water. 3. Cover the jug and leave both overnight.
flow.say: We are doing the chuna water test again, with a new question. Tonight we soak the moong and make chuna water.
flow.kid: Help soak the moong. A grown-up makes the chuna water.
flow.wait: Leave the moong and the chuna water overnight.

flow.do: Tell your child the plan. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Both dabbas will have sprouts this time. One goes in the fridge. One stays on the shelf. Which chuna water will go more milky? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One dabba goes in the fridge. One stays out. Which goes more milky? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: The shelf one, because cold makes sprouts slow.
The fridge one, because cold makes things cloudy.
The same, because both have sprouts.

flow.do: 1. Lay a wet cloth in each dabba. 2. Share the soaked moong equally between them. 3. Stand a small glass of clear chuna water in each, the same amount. 4. Close both lids tightly. 5. Put one dabba in the fridge and one on a shelf.
flow.say: Same sprouts, same cloth, same chuna water. Only the place is different.
flow.kid: Share the sprouts equally. Close the lids. One goes in the fridge.
flow.wait: Leave both dabbas for three hours.

flow.do: 1. Take the fridge dabba out. 2. Open both dabbas. 3. Hold the two glasses side by side in front of the dark cloth.
flow.say: Look at the two glasses. Which one is more milky?
flow.kid: Look at both glasses. Which one is more milky?

ask.q: Which one went more milky?
good: The shelf one.
The fridge one is still almost clear.

flow.parent: The shelf glass is usually clearly more milky. The fridge glass stays clear or only a little cloudy. Cold slows down breathing in sprouts. If both look the same, leave both for three more hours and look again.

flow.do: Ask your child what they think, what they saw and why. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Why do you think the cold sprouts made less milky water?
flow.kid: Why was the fridge water less milky? Say what you think.

ask.q: Why are fruits and vegetables kept in the fridge?
good: So they breathe slowly and stay fresh longer.
Because cold slows them down.

flow.parent: Picked fruits and vegetables are still alive and still breathing. They use up their stored food as they breathe. In the cold they breathe slowly, so they stay fresh longer.

check.q: The shelf sprouts made the chuna water more milky than the fridge sprouts. What does this show?
options: Sprouts breathe more slowly in the cold
The fridge has no air in it
check.why: Both dabbas had the same sprouts and the same air. The cold sprouts were still alive, and they would grow again when warm. They breathed out less carbon dioxide because cold slows down their breathing.

activities.title: Sure or Not Sure? Sorting tricky cases
activities.context: In this activity you sort tricky things from the house into alive, once alive and never alive. Then you put the ones you are not sure about in a bowl, and plan a test for one of them.

materials.item: three plates with paper labels: a smiling sprout (alive), a leaf with a tick (once alive), a stone (never alive)
an empty bowl with a paper label: a question mark (not sure)

tricky things from the house: a dry moong seed, a soaked moong sprout, a spoon of curd in a katori, a potato, a cotton thread, a cooked grain of rice, a phone, a steel spoon, a piece of dry coconut shell, a drawing of a cloud (draw one on paper)

schedule.what: Sort 10 tricky things onto three plates and a not-sure bowl. Plan one test.

activities.record: Draw the not-sure bowl and write the test you would do for one thing in it.

flow.do: 1. Put out the three plates and the bowl. 2. Show your child each label.
flow.say: This plate is for things that are alive now. This one is for things that were once alive. This one is for things that were never alive. The bowl is for things you are not sure about.
flow.kid: Three plates and a bowl. Alive. Once alive. Never alive. Not sure.

flow.do: 1. Hand your child one thing at a time. 2. Ask which sign of life they can see, or which is missing. 3. Let them put it on a plate or in the bowl.
flow.say: Where does this go? Which sign of life tells you? If you are not sure, it can go in the bowl.
flow.kid: Pick up one thing. Which sign of life does it show? Choose a plate or the bowl.

ask.q: Why does the phone go on the never alive plate?
good: The phone senses touch, but never eats or grows.
Phones don't have baby phones.

ask.q: Where does the cooked rice go?
good: Once alive, because rice grains came from a rice plant, but cooking killed them.

flow.parent: Let the reasons come first and don't correct straight away. The dry moong, the sprout and the potato are alive. Curd is a food full of living bacteria, so it goes on the alive plate or in the bowl. Cotton thread, cooked rice and coconut shell were once alive. The phone, the spoon and the cloud were never alive.

flow.do: Pick one thing from the not-sure bowl. Plan a test together.
flow.say: Let's choose one thing from the bowl. How could we test if it is alive? Which sign of life could we look for?
flow.kid: Pick one thing from the bowl. How can you test it?

ask.q: How could we test the dry moong seed?
good: Give the seed water and see if they sprout.
Shut the seeds in a dabba with chuna water.

ask.q: How could we test the curd?
good: Put a spoon in warm milk and see if more curd grows.

flow.parent: A good test looks for one sign of life the thing can show at home: growing (water a seed), breathing (chuna water), or having young (curd setting milk).

activities.title: Ant Watch: which signs of life can you see?
activities.context: In this activity you put a few grains of sugar near some ants and watch for five minutes. You tick each sign of life you see.

materials.item: a few grains of sugar
a small piece of paper
a sheet of paper with seven lines, one for each sign of life: you draw a small picture or write the word on each line, for ticking
a pencil

schedule.what: Draw the seven-line sheet. Put sugar near ants. Watch for five minutes. Tick each sign of life you see.

activities.record: Tick the signs you saw. Draw one ant carrying sugar.

flow.do: 1. Draw seven lines on a sheet of paper. On each line, write or draw one sign of life: eat, breathe, grow, move, sense, get rid of waste, have young. 2. Find a line of ants in the kitchen, on a windowsill or on the balcony. 3. Put a few grains of sugar on a small paper near them.
flow.say: Let's give the ants some sugar. Then we watch and look for signs of life.
flow.kid: Find some ants. Put sugar near them on a paper.
flow.parent: Almost every flat has ants somewhere. If you cannot find any, watch a crow or a pigeon at the window, or a pet, for five minutes instead.

flow.do: Watch together for five minutes. Your child ticks each sign they see.
flow.say: Watch closely. Can you see an ant move? Sense the sugar? Eat or carry food?
flow.kid: Watch the ants. Tick each sign of life you see.

ask.q: How did the ants find the sugar?
good: They smelled the sugar with their feelers.
One ant found the sugar and others followed.

flow.parent: Ants smell with their antennae, the two feelers on their head. You may see one ant find the sugar and more ants arrive soon after. Ants leave a smell trail for others to follow.

flow.do: Count the ticks together. Ask which signs you could not see.
flow.say: Which signs did you see? Which ones did you not see? Does that mean the ants don't do them?
flow.kid: Count your ticks. Which signs did you not see?

ask.q: You did not see the ants breathe. Are they breathing?
good: Yes, every living being breathes. We just can't see it.

flow.parent: Ants breathe through tiny holes along their sides, too small to see. Not seeing a sign is not the same as it not happening, which is what the chuna water test showed with the sprouts.

activities.title: The Still Minute: what keeps going when you sit still?
activities.context: In this activity you sit as still as a seed for one minute. Then you find the signs of life that kept going in your body anyway.

materials.item: a clock or phone timer

schedule.what: Sit still for one minute. Count your breaths. List what kept going.

activities.record: Draw yourself sitting still, with arrows to the parts that kept working.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to sit cross-legged and be as still as they can. 2. Time one minute. 3. Ask them to count their breaths silently.
flow.say: Sit as still as a seed for one minute. Don't move at all. Count your breaths in your head.
flow.kid: Sit as still as a seed. Count your breaths quietly.
flow.parent: Most children of seven breathe about 18 to 30 times in a minute when sitting quietly.

flow.do: Ask what kept going inside, even though they were still.
flow.say: You did not move. But what kept going inside you?
flow.kid: You sat still. What kept going inside you?

ask.q: What kept going?
good: My breathing.
My heart kept beating.
I blinked.
My tummy made a sound.

flow.parent: Breathing and the heartbeat never stop. Hair and nails keep growing too, very slowly. So being still is not the same as doing nothing. This is how it is for the sprouts as well.

setup.caption: 1. Sit as still as a seed for one minute.

setup.art: The same child with small arrows drawn to the chest, the heart, the eyes and the hair.
setup.caption: 2. Find what kept going inside you.

activities.title: Sleeping Leaves (if you have a park or a tree-lined road nearby)
activities.context: In this activity you look at the leaves of a rain tree once in the afternoon and once after sunset. Rain tree leaves fold up in the evening.

materials.item: a rain tree in a park or on your road (in many Indian cities, such as Bengaluru, Chennai, Kolkata and Mumbai)
a phone camera or paper and pencil

schedule.what: Look at rain tree leaves in the afternoon and again after sunset. Draw or photograph both times.

activities.record: Draw a small rain tree leaf in the afternoon and after sunset, side by side.

flow.do: 1. In the afternoon, find a rain tree. 2. Look at one small leaf closely. 3. Draw it or take a photo.
flow.say: This is a rain tree. Look at the tiny leaflets on this leaf. Are they open or closed?
flow.kid: Look at the tiny leaves. Are they open or closed? Draw them.
flow.parent: A rain tree is a big shady tree with a wide umbrella shape and feathery leaves made of many small leaflets. Rain trees have fluffy pink flowers in summer. Many Indian cities planted them along roads.

flow.do: 1. Go back after sunset with a torch. 2. Look at the same leaves. 3. Draw them or photograph them again.
flow.say: Look at the same leaves now, after sunset. What has changed?
flow.kid: Look again after sunset. What changed?

ask.q: What did the leaves do?
good: They folded up.
The little leaves closed together.

flow.parent: Rain tree leaflets fold together in the evening and on cloudy days, and open again in the morning light. This is a plant moving, and sensing light. No rain tree near you? Skip this activity.

projects.title: The Potato Maze: can a potato shoot find the light?
projects.context: In this three-week project you put a sprouting potato in a shoebox with walls inside and one hole at the end. You watch whether the potato's shoot finds the way to the light.

materials.item: a potato that has already started to sprout small shoots (or an old potato left in a dark cupboard for two weeks first)
a shoebox with a lid
two pieces of card from an old box, cut to fit across the shoebox
tape and scissors, for the grown-up
a small steel katori of damp soil, or a damp cloth for the potato to sit on

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the card and the hole. Do not eat the shoots or any green part of the potato, because they can make people sick.

schedule.what: Make the maze in the shoebox. Put the potato at the far end. Close the lid and put the box by a bright window, hole towards the light.
Open the lid quickly. Draw the shoots. Close it again.
Look again. Which way are the shoots going? Draw them.
Has a shoot come out of the hole? Draw the whole path.

projects.record: Draw the maze from above on day 1, 7, 14 and 21, with the shoots drawn in.

flow.do: 1. Cut a hole the size of a coin in one short end of the shoebox. 2. Tape the two card walls across the box, one from each side, each leaving a gap. 3. Put the potato at the far end, on damp soil or a damp cloth. 4. Close the lid. 5. Put the box by a bright window, hole facing the light.
flow.say: The only light comes in through this hole. The potato is at the other end, behind two walls. Will the shoots find the way out?
flow.kid: The potato sits at the dark end. Light comes in the hole. Guess: will the shoots find it?

ask.q: What do you think the shoots will do? Why?
good: Grow round the walls to the hole, because they sense the light.
Grow straight up, because they can't see.

flow.wait: Leave the box closed for a week.
flow.parent: If your potato has no shoots yet, leave it in a dark cupboard for two weeks first, and start the project once it has small shoots.

flow.do: Open the lid quickly, look, draw, and close it again.
flow.say: Look quickly, so we let in only a little light. Which way are the shoots growing?
flow.kid: Peep in quickly. Which way are the shoots going? Draw them.
flow.parent: Shoots usually grow towards the gap in the first wall. If there are no shoots after a week, keep the box somewhere warmer. Check that the soil or cloth is still damp. If it is dry, add one spoon of water.
flow.wait: Leave the box closed for another week.

flow.do: Look again and draw.
flow.say: Have the shoots gone round the first wall?
flow.kid: Look again. Have the shoots gone round a wall?
flow.wait: Leave the box closed for one more week.

flow.do: Look at the whole path the shoot took. Talk about it.
flow.say: Did a shoot come out of the hole? How did the potato find the way?
flow.kid: Did a shoot come out of the hole? How did the potato find the way?

ask.q: Which signs of life did the potato show?
good: Grew, moved, sensed the light.
Used stored food to grow.

flow.parent: Shoots often reach the hole in two to four weeks. The potato senses the faint light and grows that way, round each wall. The potato also uses up stored food, so the potato gets soft and wrinkly. If no shoot has reached the hole by day 21, leave the box one more week. Slow is a real result too.

challenges.title: Catch a Plant Moving
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Plants move too slowly for our eyes. You invent a way to catch a plant moving, and try your idea on a potted plant.
challenges.problem: A plant moves so slowly that we never see the movement happen. How could you prove that a potted plant moved, from one day to the next?
constraints: Do not hurt the plant or pull any leaf.
Your way must show the movement to someone else.
materials: a potted plant, such as a money plant, tulsi or a bean seedling
a phone camera, if you have one
a thin stick or a straw
general: Take a photo from the exact same spot every few hours, and compare the photos.
Tape a paper behind the plant and mark where a leaf tip is, then mark it again the next day.
Turn the pot away from the window, and see if the leaves turn back.
creative: Tape a thin straw to a leaf tip as a pointer, so a small movement shows as a bigger one at the end of the straw.
Shine a torch on the plant at night so the leaf's shadow falls on the wall, then mark the shadow's tip every hour.
In about 1880, Charles Darwin and his son Francis put dots on a glass sheet over a growing shoot, every hour or so. Joined up, the dots showed the shoot tip moving round in little circles.
challenges.your_turn: Choose your own way to catch the plant moving. Set it up today. Check it tomorrow, and show someone what you found.

flow.do: Read the problem to your child. Ask for ideas before showing any.
flow.say: Plants move, but too slowly for our eyes. How could we prove this plant moved by tomorrow?
flow.kid: Plants move very slowly. How can you catch this plant moving?

ask.q: What ideas do you have?
good: Take a photo now and tomorrow.
Mark where a leaf is.

flow.do: Help your child set up their idea. Read out the usual and creative ideas if they get stuck.
flow.say: Let's set up your idea. How will we know exactly where the leaf was today?
flow.kid: Set up your idea. Mark where the leaf is today.
flow.parent: The easiest strong idea is to turn the pot half a turn, so the leaves face the room, and photograph it from a fixed spot. Over one or two days, the leaves turn back towards the window.

flow.do: The next day, check together and compare.
flow.say: Did the plant move? How do you know?
flow.kid: Did the plant move? Show me how you know.
flow.wait: Check again tomorrow, and again the day after if you see no change.

check.q: A money plant was turned away from the window. Two days later, the leaves face the window again. What does this show?
options: The plant sensed the light and moved to face the window
check.why: A plant senses light and slowly turns their leaves towards the light, by growing more on the shady side. Two signs of life together: sensing and moving.

setup.art: A money plant in a pot on a windowsill, with a paper taped on the wall behind and a pencil mark next to one leaf tip.
setup.caption: 1. Mark where a leaf tip is today.

setup.art: The same plant the next day, with a second pencil mark a little way from the first.
setup.caption: 2. Mark it again tomorrow and compare.

items.p: Draw a line from each sign of life to a picture of it.
pairs: A child feeling warm breath on a hand
A sprout getting a longer tail
A cat turning her ears to a sound
A child sweating after a run
items.why: These are the seven signs of life. Every kind of living being does all seven. A strong answer can say one more example for each sign.
items.art: Seven signs written on the left, and seven small pictures on the right, mixed up.

items.p: Which one is alive?
items.why: The sleeping dog is still, but breathing, growing and alive. The fan moves and the cloud grows, but neither eats, breathes or has young.

items.p: A plant does not move at all.
items.why: False. Plants move slowly, mostly by growing. Shoots bend towards light, roots grow down, and a karela tendril curls round a string. A strong answer gives one example.

items.p: Sort these tricky things.
items.why: A dry seed and a potato are alive and resting: both can grow. Cotton and wood came from plants, so they were once alive. A phone and a cloud were never alive.
items.art: Six small drawings: a moong seed, a potato, a cotton shirt, a phone, a pencil and a cloud.

items.p: Draw the two dabbas from the chuna water test, after three hours. Colour the chuna water that went milky.
items.a: Two dabbas, each with a small glass. The glass in the sprout dabba is coloured white. The glass in the empty dabba is clear.
items.why: The sprouts breathed out carbon dioxide, which turned their chuna water milky. The dabba with only a wet cloth had nothing breathing in it. A strong drawing labels the sprouts.
items.art: Two empty outlines of steel dabbas side by side.

items.p: Living beings breathe out a gas called ________.
items.why: Carbon dioxide is the gas that living beings breathe out. It turns chuna water milky.

items.p: A toy car moves. How many of the seven signs of life is the toy car missing?
items.why: The car shows only one sign: moving. 7 take away 1 is 6. The car never eats, breathes, grows, senses, gets rid of waste or has young.

items.p: An old potato is left in a dark cupboard. It grows long shoots, all bent towards the crack of light at the door. Write two signs of life the potato showed.
items.a: The potato grew shoots. The shoots sensed the light and grew towards the crack of light.
items.why: A strong answer names two signs, such as growing, sensing the light, moving towards it, or using stored food, and says what the potato did for each.

items.p: Three of these are alive now. Which one is not alive now?
opts: A dry leaf lying on the road
items.why: The sprout, the crow and the mushroom eat, breathe, grow and have young. A dry leaf fell from a tree, so it was once alive, but it is not alive now.

items.p: Label this plant. Write what each part does: leaf, root, flower, shoot tip.
items.a: Leaf: makes food and breathes. Root: grows down to find water. Flower: makes seeds, the plant's young. Shoot tip: grows towards the light.
items.why: Each part shows a sign of life: eating, sensing and moving, having young, and growing. A strong answer gives a sign for each part.
items.art: A simple drawing of a small plant in a pot with four empty label lines pointing to a leaf, a root, a flower and the shoot tip.

items.p: Arjun, a boy in Class 2, wants to show that dry moong seeds are alive. Which test is best?
opts: Give the seeds water and see if they sprout
Look at the seeds under a lamp
items.why: A living seed wakes up with water and grows. Shaking or looking does not test any sign of life.

items.p: Two friends in Kochi look at a katori of curd. They argue about whether curd is alive.

views.says: Curd is food. Food is not alive.
Curd is alive. A spoon of curd turned a whole bowl of milk into curd.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with more? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both are partly right. Curd is a food, but curd is full of tiny living bacteria. The bacteria eat milk sugar, grow and make more of themselves, which is why a spoon of curd sets a bowl of milk.
items.why: The curd itself is not one living being, but it holds millions of living beings. A strong answer uses the milk-setting evidence.

items.p: Put an onion on top of a glass of water, so its bottom just touches the water. What do you think you will see after a few days? Which sign of life would it show?
items.a: White roots grow down into the water, and a green shoot may grow from the top. This shows growing, and the roots reaching into the water show sensing.
items.why: A strong answer says what we would see and names a sign of life. The onion has stored food, like the potato, so it can grow.

items.p: Sprouts in the fridge breathe out more carbon dioxide than sprouts on a warm shelf.
items.why: False. Cold slows down breathing. The fridge sprouts breathe out less carbon dioxide, so their chuna water stays clearer.

items.p: Put the steps of the chuna water test in order.
items: Close both lids and wait three hours
Make chuna water and let it settle overnight
Put sprouts in one dabba and only a wet cloth in the other
Compare the two glasses against a dark cloth
a: Make chuna water and let it settle overnight
Put sprouts in one dabba and only a wet cloth in the other
Close both lids and wait three hours
Compare the two glasses against a dark cloth
items.why: First make the chuna water, then set up the two dabbas, then wait, then compare.

items.p: Match each tricky thing to the reason for its answer.
pairs: Senses touch, but never grows: never alive
Looks still, but sprouts with water: alive
Grows, but never eats: never alive
Came from a tree: once alive
items.why: Each answer comes from checking the signs of life one by one, not from how the thing looks.

items.p: Draw a plant that senses light. Show where the light comes from and which way the plant bends.
items.a: A plant with shoots or leaves bending towards a window or a lamp.
items.why: Plants sense where the light is and grow that way. A strong drawing shows the light and the plant bending towards the light, such as a potato shoot in a maze or a money plant at a window.

items.p: A spoon of curd set a whole katori of warm milk overnight. Which sign of life did the curd bacteria show?
opts: They had young: they made more of themselves
They moved to a new house
They got rid of the milk
items.why: The bacteria ate the milk sugar, grew and split into more bacteria. Making more of their own kind is having young.

items.p: When you sit very still, you still ________ in and out.
items.why: Breathing never stops, even when you are still or asleep. The sprouts are the same.

items.p: In the chuna water test, why did we keep both dabbas in the same place for the same time?
items.a: So the only difference was the sprouts. Then we know the sprouts made the water milky.
items.why: This is a fair test. A strong answer says that if the place or time were different too, we would not know what caused the change.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 2, shut her moong sprouts in a dabba with chuna water. After three hours the water was still clear. She had not pressed the lid down tight. Why might the water still be clear? What should she do next?
items.a: Breathed-out carbon dioxide may have leaked out through the loose lid, and room air came in. She should press the lid down tight and try again.
items.why: A shut dabba keeps the carbon dioxide inside, so the chuna water can catch it. A strong answer says the loose lid let the gas out and says to repeat the test with a tight lid.

items.p: Two thinkers from long ago disagreed about plants.

views.who: Aristotle, a thinker in Greece about 2,300 years ago
views.says: Plants feed, grow and make seeds, but plants have no senses.

views.who: Jagadish Chandra Bose, a scientist in Kolkata about 120 years ago
views.says: Plants respond to touch, light and heat, much as animals do.

items.ask: Which thinker do you agree with? Use something you saw in this unit. Then say what the other thinker might answer.
items.a: A strong answer uses evidence, such as the potato shoots growing towards light, the karela tendril curling round a string, or rain tree leaves folding at night. It also gives the other side fairly: Aristotle might say these are not real senses, because plants have no eyes or ears.
items.why: Plants clearly sense light and touch and act on them. People still argue about whether this is feeling, or only reacting.

items.p: Farhan, a boy in Class 2, boils some moong, lets them cool and shuts them in a dabba with chuna water. What will happen in three hours?
opts: The chuna water goes milky fast
The moong grow long white tails
items.why: Boiling kills the moong, so they no longer breathe. With nothing breathing, the chuna water stays clear. This would make a good fair test against living sprouts.

items.p: A robot cleaner moves round the room, senses the walls and goes back to its charger when the battery is low. Which signs of life does the robot seem to have? Which are missing? Is the robot alive?
items.a: The robot seems to move and sense. Charging is a bit like eating. But the robot never breathes, grows or has baby robots. So the robot was never alive.
items.why: A strong answer goes through the signs and decides from the missing ones, not from how clever the robot seems.

items.p: If something does not move for a whole day, it cannot be alive.
items.why: False. A dry seed, a potato and a coconut can sit still for weeks and still be alive. The chuna water test showed still sprouts breathing.

items.p: Plan a test to find out if a whole coconut is alive. Draw what you would do.
items.a: A whole coconut with the husk, half buried in damp soil in a big pot, with a note to check for a green shoot every week.
items.why: A strong plan tests one sign of life the coconut can show, such as growing a shoot in damp soil. It might also say how long to wait: a coconut can take three to six months to sprout.

items.p: Which of these can make more of their own kind?
items.why: Living beings make more of their own kind: mangoes have seeds, bacteria split, and a potato grows new potatoes. A cloud can split in two, but a new cloud is not made by the old one from food. Phones and cars are made in factories.

items.p: Three of these breathe out carbon dioxide. Which one does not?
items.why: Sprouts, ants and cats are living beings, and all living beings breathe out carbon dioxide. A steel spoon was never alive.

items.p: Dry seeds are alive but resting. Seeds wake up when they get ________.
items.why: Water wakes a resting seed. The seed swells, starts breathing faster and grows a root. Warmth and air help too.

items.p: Label the parts of the chuna water test: the sprouts, the chuna water, the wet cloth and the lid.
items.a: Sprouts on the bottom, on the wet cloth. Chuna water in the small glass in the middle. The lid on top, closed tight.
items.why: A strong answer also says why each part is there: the lid keeps room air out, and the wet cloth keeps the sprouts damp.
items.art: A drawing of an open steel dabba from the side, with four empty label lines.

quiz.p: How many signs of life are there?
quiz.why: There are seven: eat, breathe, grow, move, sense, get rid of waste and have young.

quiz.p: Which of these is a sign of life?
quiz.why: Having young is one of the seven signs. Being shiny or heavy has nothing to do with being alive: a steel spoon is shiny, and a stone is heavy.

quiz.p: In the dabba test, clear chuna water turned milky next to the moong sprouts. What made it milky?
opts: Carbon dioxide breathed out by the sprouts
quiz.why: The empty dabba had the same wet cloth and stayed clear. The dabba was shut, so light did not matter. The sprouts breathed out carbon dioxide.

quiz.p: Why do plants seem still, though they are alive?
opts: Plants move slowly, mostly by growing
Plants are only pretending to be alive
quiz.why: Plants move by growing: shoots bend to light and roots grow down. This is too slow for our eyes to see. If you said plants move only at night, think of the money plant turning to the window in daytime.

quiz.p: Divya, a girl in Class 2, says, 'My toy car moves, so my car is alive.' What is wrong with her idea?
opts: Moving is not enough: the car never eats, grows or has young
A car is alive only when the engine is on
quiz.why: One sign alone does not show life. A living being does all seven signs.

quiz.p: Which of these is alive, though it seems to do nothing?
quiz.why: A dry moong seed is alive and resting. With water, the seed sprouts. A marble and a plastic spoon were never alive.

quiz.p: Why does a spoon of curd turn warm milk into curd?
opts: The curd has tiny living bacteria that grow in the milk
quiz.why: Curd bacteria eat the sugar in milk, grow and make more of themselves. As they do, the milk turns thick and sour.

quiz.p: Plants breathe in the daytime and at night.
quiz.why: True. Plants breathe all the time. In sunlight they also make food, which hides the breathing.

quiz.p: In the chuna water test, why was there a dabba with only a wet cloth?
opts: To compare: it shows what happens with no sprouts
quiz.why: The empty dabba is the same in every way except the sprouts. So any difference must be caused by the sprouts. This is a fair test.

quiz.p: Which tricky case was never alive?
quiz.why: A cloud grows and moves, but never eats, breathes or has young. A potato is alive, and curd is full of living bacteria.

quiz.p: A karela vine on a balcony touches a string with a thin tendril. The tendril curls tightly round the string. Which sign of life is this?
quiz.why: The tendril senses the touch of the string and curls round it. That is sensing, and moving too.

applications: Fruits and vegetables keep fresh longer in the fridge, because cold slows down their breathing, so they use up their stored food more slowly.
Farmers and grain shops keep grain dry. Damp grain wakes up and breathes, which warms the grain and makes it spoil.
Families set curd every day with a spoon of yesterday's curd, because the living bacteria in that curd make more curd.
Scientists looking for life on other planets look for signs of life, such as gases that living beings make.

open_questions.q: Do plants feel anything, the way we feel?
open_questions.why_open: Plants clearly sense light, touch, water and even sound, and they change what they do. Many scientists say plants feel and decide in their own way. Others say plants only react automatically, because plants have no brain. The argument is not settled.

open_questions.q: How long can a resting seed stay alive?
open_questions.why_open: Seeds of a date palm about 2,000 years old, found in Israel, were planted in 2005, and one grew into a tree. Nobody knows the longest a seed can rest and still wake up.

open_questions.q: If there is life on other planets, would we know it when we saw it?
open_questions.why_open: Our seven signs come from life on Earth. Life somewhere else might be very different, and might not show the signs in a way we would notice.

Is a plant near you breathing right now? How do you know?

maths.problem: A toy car shows one sign of life: moving. A cloud shows two: growing and moving. A crow shows all seven. How many more signs does the crow show than the cloud?
maths.explain: The crow shows 7 signs and the cloud shows 2. 7 take away 2 is 5. So the crow shows 5 more signs than the cloud.
maths.context: This is about counting the signs of life in the tricky cases game.
maths.why_maths: Counting the signs a thing has, and the signs it is missing, helps us decide if something is alive.

maths.problem: In the ant watch, Anjana, a girl in Class 2, counted ants reaching the sugar. In the first minute, 2 ants came. In the second minute, 5 came. In the third minute, 9 came. What pattern do you see, and why do you think more ants came each minute?
maths.answer: More ants came every minute: 2, then 5, then 9.
maths.explain: Each minute more ants came than the minute before. One ant found the sugar and left a smell trail. Other ants followed the trail, and more and more found the sugar.
maths.context: This is about the ant watch, where you put sugar near some ants.
maths.why_maths: Writing the count for each minute shows a pattern, and the pattern tells us something about how ants find food.

maths.problem: In the story, one potato made 7 new potatoes. Shalini plants 3 of the new potatoes. If each one makes 5 new potatoes, how many new potatoes will there be?
maths.explain: 3 potatoes, each making 5. That is 3 groups of 5: 5, 10, 15. So there will be 15 new potatoes.
maths.context: This is about the potato in the story, which had young.
maths.why_maths: Equal groups show how fast living beings can make more of themselves.

maths.problem: In the dabba test, half a cup of sprouts made the chuna water milky in about 3 hours. Nandini, a girl in Class 2, thinks one whole cup of sprouts in the same dabba would make it milky faster. Do you agree? About how long might it take?
maths.answer: Yes. About half the time, so about 1 and a half hours.
maths.explain: Twice as many sprouts breathe out about twice as much carbon dioxide each hour. So the same milky colour would come in about half the time. Half of 3 hours is 1 and a half hours. This is a guess, so test it to check.
maths.context: This is about the chuna water test with moong sprouts.
maths.why_maths: Estimating helps us make a guess with a reason before we test it.

science: Germinating seeds respire and release carbon dioxide, which turns limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) milky as calcium carbonate forms. A standard school experiment, for example NCERT Science.
Respiration rate in plant tissue falls steeply with temperature, which is why cold storage keeps produce fresh longer.
Plants respire day and night. In light, photosynthesis takes in more carbon dioxide than respiration gives out.
Joseph Priestley, 1771, a sprig of mint restoring air in which a candle had burned out (Experiments and Observations on Different Kinds of Air).
Jan Ingenhousz, Experiments upon Vegetables, Discovering Their Great Power of Purifying the Common Air in the Sun-shine, and of Injuring it in the Shade and at Night (London, 1779).

Kamala Sohonie (1911 to 1998): admitted to the Indian Institute of Science in 1933 after first being refused because she was a woman; PhD at Cambridge (1939) on the respiratory enzymes of potato and other plant tissue, including cytochrome c.
Potato shoots are phototropic; the potato maze is a long-standing school demonstration. Sprouted seed potatoes typically yield several new tubers in about three months.
Samanea saman (rain tree) leaflets fold at dusk and in cloudy weather (nyctinasty).
Tendrils of cucurbits such as bitter gourd coil after contact with a support (thigmotropism).
Charles Darwin, assisted by Francis Darwin, The Power of Movement in Plants (1880): circumnutation traced as dots on glass plates.
Aristotle, De Anima, Book 2: plants have the nutritive soul (nutrition, growth, reproduction) but not perception.
Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, the dialogue of Bhrigu and Bharadvaja on the life of trees (section 184 in K. M. Ganguli's translation).
Prashna Upanishad, Question 2: the dispute of the senses and the life-breath (prana).
Judean date palm grown from a roughly 2,000-year-old seed from Masada, germinated in 2005 (Sallon and others, Science, 2008).

roots.context: We have tested sprouts, potatoes, curd and tricky cases for the signs of life. Now we ask what the still, breathing sprouts tell us about being alive.

deep_truth.truth: Moong sprouts lay still in a shut dabba, yet their chuna water went milky. The dabba with only a wet cloth stayed clear. Your own breath turned chuna water milky in the same way. So sprouts that seem to do nothing are breathing all the time, just as you are.
deep_truth.habit: We decide what is alive by whether we see it move. Breathing goes on inside every living being, with no movement we can see.
deep_truth.evidence: In the chuna water test, the chuna water next to the sprouts went milky, like the glass you blew into, and the empty dabba stayed clear. In the cold sprouts test, sprouts in the fridge breathed more slowly but were still alive.

three.who_am_i: You are a breathing being, like the sprouts. Even when you sit still or sleep, you keep breathing.
three.what_is_life: Life is something a body keeps doing, all the time, even when nothing seems to happen. The sprouts and the potato were busy while they lay still.
three.what_is_this_world: The carbon dioxide you breathe out goes into the air of your room. Plants take it in through their leaves and build it into new leaves.

roots.thread: Your breath and the sprouts' breath both turned chuna water milky. The same gas, carbon dioxide, comes out of every breathing being: you, an ant, a sleeping cat and a sprout. Plants take that gas in through their leaves, and use sunlight to build it into food and new leaves. So the air in your flat passes from one living being to another, all day long. Every one of them senses and acts in their own way.

teachings.teaching: The senses, such as speech, sight, hearing and the mind, once argued about which of them holds up the body. The life-breath, called prana, began to leave. At once all the others had to leave too, like bees that rise when their leader rises. When prana settled, they all settled. So the senses saw that the quiet breath holds everything up.
teachings.link: In our test, the sprouts lay still and seemed to do nothing. But their breathing went on, quietly, under everything else. Breathing is a sign of life that goes on all the time.

teachings.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, the talk between the sages Bhrigu and Bharadvaja
teachings.teaching: Bhrigu teaches that trees are alive and sense the world. Their leaves and flowers fade in heat, so they feel warmth. A creeper finds a tree to climb, so the creeper senses the way. Trees drink water through their roots.
teachings.link: We saw this in the potato shoots reaching for the crack of light, and in a karela tendril curling round a string. Plants sense the world and act on it, though they seem still.

science.text: All living beings breathe, plants included, day and night. Moong sprouts in a shut dabba give out enough carbon dioxide to turn chuna water milky in a few hours.
Plants sense light, touch, water and warmth and change what they do. Whether plants also feel what happens to them is still argued about.

other_view.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker, and many scientists today
other_view.view: Aristotle taught that plants feed, grow and make seeds, but have no senses at all. Many scientists today agree that plants sense the world, but they say plants react automatically, because plants have no brain.

practice.title: Still as a seed, breathing
practice.say: Sit very still, like a seed in a packet. Hold your palm in front of your mouth. Breathe out slowly and feel the warm air on your hand. Breathe in slowly and feel the air go in. You are not moving, but your breath is. Now look at a plant or a sprout near you. Plants are breathing quietly too.
practice.kid: Sit as still as a seed. Hold your palm in front of your mouth. Breathe out slowly and feel the warm air. Plants and sprouts are breathing too.

ask: If breathing never stops, is anything in a living body ever really still?
The air you breathe out goes into a plant. Is part of you now in the plant?

how_we_found_out.story: About 250 years ago, scientists found that green plants can make stale air fresh again. In 1771, Joseph Priestley, in England, put a sprig of mint in a closed jar of air in which a candle had burned out. After some days, a candle could burn in that air again. So many people thought plants only clean the air, and never spoil it the way breathing animals do. In 1779, Jan Ingenhousz, a Dutch doctor working in England, tested plants in sunlight and in the dark. In sunlight, green leaves made the air fresh. But in the dark, the same plants made the air stale, just as a breathing animal does. Roots, flowers and fruits made the air stale even in sunlight. So plants breathe, all the time. In the 1930s, Kamala Sohonie, an Indian scientist working at Cambridge University in England, studied potatoes. She found in plant cells a substance that animal cells also use when they breathe.
how_we_found_out.who: Jan Ingenhousz, a Dutch doctor, and Kamala Sohonie, an Indian scientist, after Joseph Priestley's work in England
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That plants only make the air fresh, and do not breathe the way animals do.

Made the soaked moong step honest about tails, added the potato lead time and a dampness check, and made the plant-moving check one or two days.
